## Purpose

This SOP describes the complete workflow for preparing geological rock
samples and analyzing their major-element oxide composition by
wavelength-dispersive X-ray fluorescence (WD-XRF). The procedure covers
sample powdering, flux fusion bead preparation, bead polishing, and
instrument operation on the PANalytical XRF spectrometer using the
SuperQ software with the "Geology Beads" application [@norrish1969;
@claisse2003; @panalytical_superq].


## Scope

- **Applies to:** Rock, mineral, and geological samples analyzed as
  lithium tetraborate fusion beads for major-element oxide determination
  (e.g., SiO~2~, Al~2~O~3~, Fe~2~O~3~, CaO, MgO, Na~2~O, K~2~O,
  TiO~2~, P~2~O~5~, MnO)
- **Does not apply to:** Pressed-pellet trace-element analysis,
  handheld (portable) XRF measurements, or non-geological materials
- **Locations:** Rock preparation lab (powdering and polishing);
  analytical lab / wet lab (weighing, fusion); XRF lab (instrument
  operation)

## Definitions

- **Certified reference material (CRM):** A geological standard with
  certified major-element oxide concentrations from an accredited
  producer (e.g., NIST, USGS, BCR); used to verify XRF accuracy
  during each analytical session [@norrish1969].
- **Detection limit (MDL):** The lowest concentration of an element
  reliably detected above background; varies by element, matrix, and
  instrument settings; typically 1--50 mg/kg for common elements by
  WD-XRF.
- **Flux (dilithium tetraborate, Li~2~B~4~O~7~):** A reagent mixed
  with the rock powder in a 2:1 (flux:sample) ratio; lowers the
  melting point and produces a homogeneous glass bead that eliminates
  mineralogical matrix effects during analysis [@claisse2003].
- **Fluorescence (X-ray):** The emission of characteristic X-rays from
  a sample excited by primary X-rays; each element emits at unique
  energies that identify and quantify it [@norrish1969].
- **Fundamental parameters (FP) method:** An XRF calibration approach
  that uses known physical constants to calculate element concentrations
  from measured fluorescence intensities without matrix-matched
  standards for every sample type.
- **Fusion bead:** A glass disc produced by melting the powdered rock
  sample with lithium tetraborate flux at 1000 °C; the homogeneous
  glass eliminates mineralogical matrix effects [@claisse2003].
- **Geology Beads:** The SuperQ application/archive configured for
  major-element oxide analysis of fusion beads on the PANalytical XRF
  spectrometer [@panalytical_superq].
- **K-alpha and K-beta lines:** The most commonly measured
  characteristic X-ray emission lines for elements; produced when an
  electron is ejected from the K shell and replaced from the L or M
  shell, respectively.
- **Loss on ignition (LOI):** The mass percentage lost when a
  pre-weighed rock powder is heated to 1000 °C; reflects H~2~O,
  CO~2~, and organic matter content; used as a correction in
  major-element summation [@norrish1969].
- **Matrix effects:** Absorption and enhancement of X-ray signals by
  other elements in the sample; minimized by the flux fusion method
  [@claisse2003].
- **Shatterbox:** A vibratory ring-and-puck mill used to grind rock
  chips to a fine powder suitable for fusion.
- **SuperQ:** The PANalytical software used to control the XRF
  spectrometer, define measurement sequences, and retrieve results
  [@panalytical_superq].
- **WD-XRF (wavelength-dispersive XRF):** An XRF configuration in
  which characteristic X-rays are separated by a crystal monochromator
  before detection; provides higher spectral resolution and lower
  detection limits than energy-dispersive (ED-XRF) systems.
- **X-ray fluorescence (XRF):** A non-destructive elemental analysis
  technique in which a sample excited by a primary X-ray beam emits
  characteristic fluorescent X-rays that are measured to determine
  elemental composition [@norrish1969].


## Safety and Hazards

::: {.callout-warning}
### Hazards

- **High-temperature furnace:** The muffle furnace operates at 1000 °C.
  Crucibles and tiles removed from the furnace are extremely hot. Do
  not touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled.
- **Compressed air:** Loud; wear ear protection when blowing out
  equipment.
- **Rock chipper:** Flying rock fragments are common. Always wear
  safety glasses. Never look into the chipper while it is running.
- **Shatterbox:** The unit vibrates intensely and can travel across the
  floor. Get help repositioning it if needed.
- **Chemical reagents:** Dilithium tetraborate flux is a fine powder;
  avoid inhalation. Ethanol is flammable.
- **X-ray radiation:** The XRF instrument contains an X-ray source.
  Follow all posted radiation safety procedures. Do not open the
  instrument lid while the arm is moving or the flap is up.
:::

### Required PPE

- [ ] Safety glasses (required in the rock prep lab at all times)
- [ ] Laboratory coat
- [ ] Nitrile gloves (powder handling and polishing)
- [ ] Ear protection (when using the shatterbox or compressed air)
- [ ] Heat-resistant gloves (when handling crucibles or the tile from
      the furnace)

### Emergency Procedures

Do not work in the lab without letting someone know your plans and
estimated return time. Phones and safety showers are in all labs.
Refer to [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)
for all emergency procedures.


## Prerequisites and Required Reading

- [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)

::: {.callout-important}
Minimize contamination at every step. Wear gloves, clean equipment
thoroughly between samples, and assume any shared equipment is dirty
unless you just cleaned it. Leave the lab and equipment cleaner than
you found it.
:::

## Procedure

### Step 1: Powdering the Sample

A complete fusion batch is 9 samples. If you plan fusions, turn on the
furnace first (see §6.3) since it takes about 1 hour to reach 1000 °C.

#### Chipping

1. Use the rock chipper to reduce each sample to pieces smaller than
   approximately 1 cm. Wear safety glasses. Clean the chipper jaws
   thoroughly between samples with compressed air and an ethanol wipe.
2. Weigh out approximately 20--30 g of chipped material into a labeled
   sample bag.

#### Shatterbox Milling

3. Place a piece of brown butcher paper under the shatterbox head
   assembly to catch any spillage.
4. Wipe all shatterbox bowl components (ring, puck, and bowl) with an
   ethanol-dampened Kimwipe. Allow to dry completely.
5. Load the chipped sample into the tungsten carbide bowl. Do not
   overfill (maximum ~two-thirds full).
6. Lock the lid and run the shatterbox for 60--90 seconds. Longer
   milling times reduce particle size further.
7. Unlock the lid and carefully transfer the powder onto white printer
   paper, keeping all components on the paper edge so exterior metal
   surfaces do not contact the sample. Funnel the powder into the
   labeled container. Use a fresh sheet of paper for every sample.

#### Cleaning the Shatterbox

8. If powder is stuck, scrub with a green Brillo pad. If that is
   insufficient, run a scoop of sand for 15 seconds and discard.
9. Detail all pieces with compressed air (hold pieces in the airflow;
   scrub with the Brillo pad). **Do not let the metal hose tip touch
   any bowl surface.** Use ear protection.
10. Finish with an ethanol wipe on a Kimwipe. After the last sample,
    clean up, recycle paper, replace the bowl, and turn off the
    shatterbox.


### Step 2: Weighing and Mixing

1. Bring your powdered samples to the analytical lab. Get an XRF
   sample sheet from the drawer left of the weigh station, fill out
   the top portion, and keep it on a wooden tray next to the balance.
2. Retrieve a small cup of flux from the desiccator.
3. For each sample:
   a. Label a plastic cup lid with the sample number.
   b. Place the cup (no lid) in the cardboard holder on the balance,
      close the sliding door, and zero.
   c. Weigh 3.5000 g (±0.0004 g) of sample powder. Record the exact
      mass. Zero the balance.
   d. Add 7.0000 g (±0.0004 g) of flux (2:1 flux-to-sample ratio)
      [@claisse2003]. Record the mass. If you add too much flux, remove
      the excess but **do not return it to the reagent container**.
   e. Seal the lid tightly.
4. Mix each cup on the Vortex mixer for about one minute. If powder
   clings to the sides, pass the deionizing bar over the cup.


### Step 3: First Fusion {#sec-first-fusion}

#### Furnace Startup

1. Flip the black switch on the front of the furnace.
2. Press the T1 temperature button and confirm T = 1000 °C.
3. Set a duration (e.g., 24, 48, or 72 hours). Press Enter and Start.
   It takes roughly 1 hour to reach 1000 °C.

::: {.callout-caution}
Do not spill glass in the furnace or introduce liquids. Do not use
this furnace for temperatures below 500 °C -- use a regular drying
oven instead. Do not shut off the furnace mid-cycle with the power
button; let it run out its programmed time and shut off automatically.
:::

#### Loading Crucibles

4. Select 9 graphite crucibles from the drawer under the furnace.
   Clean each inside by gently wiping with a Kimwipe and blowing out
   with compressed air.
5. Back at the analytical lab, carefully empty each cup into the
   corresponding crucible. **Maintaining the correct order is critical
   -- once the powder is in the crucible, there is no way to tell
   samples apart.**
6. Place the empty cups (lids on) in the box labeled "Dirty Cups for
   Blowing Out."

#### Fusing

7. In the wet lab, place a tile on the brick stand (small hole facing
   toward you) and crank the stand up until the tile is about halfway
   up the side of the furnace.
8. Put on both long heat-resistant gloves. Using the tongs, slide the
   tile into the furnace. Close the door as quickly as possible.
9. Wait 20--30 minutes for the furnace to recover to 1000 °C, then
   leave the samples for 10--15 minutes. Longer fusion times help
   carbon-rich samples degas fully.

::: {.callout-danger}
The tile and crucibles are extremely hot when removed from the furnace.
Do not touch them, even with gloves, until fully cooled.
:::

10. Wearing gloves, open the furnace and carefully pull the tile out
    using the tongs and the tile hole. Move the tile to the hot plate
    and close the furnace.


### Step 4: Regrinding and Second Fusion

1. Once the crucibles are cool enough to handle, pour the first-fusion
   glass back into the shatterbox bowl. Re-grind for 60 seconds.
2. Return the powder to the crucible and re-fuse at 1000 °C for
   15--20 minutes to remove any remaining bubbles and produce a
   homogeneous bead.
3. Once cooled, inspect each bead visually. Beads should be clear,
   bubble-free glass covering the full crucible bottom. If a bead
   has a dark carbon pellet at the bottom, fuse for an additional
   15 minutes.


### Step 5: Polishing the Bead

Polish the flat (analytical) surface of each bead on the 4-stage
grinding/polishing laps to remove surface scratches and contamination
that would scatter X-rays.

1. Use the coarsest lap first (e.g., 600 grit SiC), working through
   progressively finer stages.
2. After each stage, clean the bead in the ultrasonic cleaner with
   distilled water (3 minutes).
3. After the final lap, inspect the flat surface under the lab light;
   it must be mirror-smooth with no visible scratches.
4. Label each bead on the curved (non-analytical) side using a
   diamond-tipped pen or rotary tool.


### Step 6: XRF Analysis

1. Open a "Measure and Analyze" window from the SuperQ Manager.
   Wear gloves and avoid touching the flat (analytical) surface of the
   bead [@panalytical_superq].
2. Click the multi-cup icon to open the Sample Changer. Double-click
   position A1. Enter the sample name; set type to "Routine,"
   application to "Geology Beads," priority to "Normal," and verify
   weights are correct. Click **Add**. Available positions are A1--A8
   and B5--B8.
3. Once all samples are entered, click **Measure**.

::: {.callout-note}
If the XRF has not been running recently, the instrument needs to warm
up until the front-panel readouts display 60 and 50. Run the first
bead until those values are reached, then click Abort. Wait for the
arm to return the sample, then restart. Running samples before warm-up
can compromise the analysis [@panalytical_superq].
:::


### Step 7: Retrieving Results

1. Open a "Results Evaluation" window. Set the archive to "Geology
   Beads" and adjust the date range. Use the "Name Mask" field to
   filter results. Click on a sample and then click "View."
2. To export data: open a "Results Quantitative" window. Adjust date
   and name mask. Click the Print icon, then "Delimited Values Report"
   to clipboard. Paste into a spreadsheet.


## Quality Control

- Verify the 2:1 flux-to-sample ratio for every sample; record exact
  masses on the XRF sample sheet [@claisse2003].
- Visually inspect beads before loading; reject cracked, broken, or
  bubble-compromised beads.
- Run at least one CRM alongside unknowns to monitor instrument drift
  and accuracy [@norrish1969].
- If a bead required a third fusion, note this on the sample sheet.


## Cleanup Checklist

- [ ] All paper recycled (butcher paper, white paper)
- [ ] Shatterbox bowl cleaned and replaced; shatterbox off
- [ ] Chipper cleaned (ethanol wipe on all contact surfaces)
- [ ] Crucibles returned to the drawer (or discarded if degraded)
- [ ] Plastic cups blown out and restocked (or discarded after 6 uses)
- [ ] Polishing laps spun dry
- [ ] Sonicator drained if not in regular use
- [ ] XRF sample sheet completed and filed
- [ ] All personal items removed from the lab
- [ ] Work surfaces wiped down


## Troubleshooting

| Symptom                                 | Possible Cause / Action                           |
|:----------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------|
| Glass does not cover crucible bottom    | Insufficient fusion time; re-fuse longer          |
| Bead cracked or has deep air bubbles    | Air trapped during fusion; re-fuse briefly        |
| Carbon pellet at bottom of bead         | Carbon not fully degassed; fuse longer next time  |
| Powder clings to plastic cup walls      | Pass the deionizing bar over the cup              |
| XRF front-panel numbers not at 60/50   | Instrument not warmed up; run a bead until ready  |
| XRF data appear anomalous               | Sample run before warm-up; re-run                 |

## Training Record

Before performing XRF sample preparation and analysis independently,
personnel must:

1. Read this SOP in full
2. Complete [SOP-L002 Laboratory Safety](SOP-L002-laboratory-safety.qmd)
   training
3. Review furnace safety instructions posted above the furnace
4. Observe a trained operator perform a complete batch (powdering
   through analysis)
5. Prepare and analyze a batch under supervision with acceptable CRM
   recovery
6. Be signed off by the lab technician or PI
